fields.Comment:
FDA approved Sunharbo (asundexian) on November 9, the first factor XIa inhibitor approved in the U.S., for use with antiplatelet therapy in adults after a recent mild-to-moderate non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA). In OCEANIC-STROKE (12,327 adults) it reduced the risk of ischemic stroke by 26% versus placebo over a median 14.2 months; overall major bleeding was similar, but higher in patients over 75 and in the first 90 days, and it is not approved for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. For Latin American payers, what evidence would matter most before adding a new class on top of the antiplatelet regimens already in use?
https://healthsignals.news/paho-study-470-million-in-the-americas-live-with-a-neurological-disorder/?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=comment&utm_campaign=fda #HealthSignals

Stojanovic et al. (Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics, 2026) add useful detail: the 413 suffix-only reports were mostly submitted directly to FDA (86.2%), commonly from Veterans Affairs medical centers and specialty pharmacies. Across all biosimilar reports, 82% named the manufacturer, compared with 42.6% of suffix-only reports carrying any manufacturer information. The authors also note the FDA naming approach diverges from other international regulators. For biosimilar developers working across the Americas, where identification conventions vary, which data points end up doing the most work in pharmacovigilance?
